prompt: In the stand-in, what is the stated confidence worked out from?

choices.text: The gap between its two best labels
choices.why: That would look at the other labels, which it never does.

choices.text: Its chosen label's evidence
choices.why: Right: 0.62 plus a tenth of that score, capped at 0.99.

choices.text: The confidences shown in the prompt's three examples
choices.why: The examples show the format; the number is computed.

choices.text: How often it was right on the test set
choices.why: It never sees the labels; that would make it calibrated by construction.

prompt: What confidence did the stand-in state for `h04`, the atlas it labelled delivery?
hint: The last field of the reply.
The message has words for two labels.

choices.text: It had no keywords, so the stand-in guessed
choices.why: It had three, two for delivery and one for returns.

choices.text: The prompt's examples told it to say 0.97
choices.why: The examples say 0.9, 0.95 and 0.85; the number is computed.

choices.text: Returns evidence went unseen
choices.why: Right: confidence from the winner's evidence alone.

choices.text: The person who labelled it was wrong
choices.why: The customer wants to return the atlas; returns is a fair label.

prompt: Why is calibration checked over many answers and never one?

choices.text: A single answer cannot refute 0.85
choices.why: Right: a stated 0.85 is a claim about a rate, and a rate needs many answers.

choices.text: Single answers have no confidence field
choices.why: Every reply here carries one.

choices.text: `pl calibrate` refuses fewer than ten replies
choices.why: It does not; it would print a thin table.

choices.text: Confidence only means something above 0.9
choices.why: Every bin makes a claim that can be checked.

prompt: The seven replies between 0.7 and 0.8 stated 0.73 on average. What share of them was right? Two decimal places.
On a reliability diagram, a bin's point sits below the diagonal. What does that say?
hint: Stated is along, accuracy is up.

choices.text: That bin said less than it achieved
choices.why: That would put the point above the line.

choices.text: The bin is too small to read
choices.why: Size is the `n` beside it, not where it sits.

choices.text: The answers in that bin did not parse
choices.why: Only parsed replies with a confidence are binned.

choices.text: Overconfident: it said more than it delivered
choices.why: Right: accuracy below the confidence it stated.

prompt: The bin below 0.7 holds two replies, both wrong. How much weight should that point carry when you read the diagram?

choices.text: The most, because its gap is the largest
choices.why: A large gap measured on two replies is mostly chance.

choices.text: Very little: two cannot show a rate
choices.why: Right: a point needs its `n` beside it.

choices.text: None, so the diagram should drop small bins
choices.why: Dropping them hides where the model may be worst; showing `n` is enough.

choices.text: Exactly as much as the bin of 34
choices.why: ECE itself weights bins by their size.

prompt: Seven replies of 70 stated 0.73 on average and were right 0.29 of the time. How much does that bin add to the ECE? Three decimal places.
hint: The bin's share of replies, times the gap.

prompt: The score that averages, over every reply, the squared difference between stated confidence and 1 or 0 is the ___ score.
hint: Named after the meteorologist who proposed it.

prompt: A model states 0.80 on every reply and is right 80% of the time. What do ECE and Brier say about it?
hint: ECE compares the number with the rate; Brier asks whether it separates right from wrong.

choices.text: Both say it is perfect
choices.why: Brier charges it 0.16, worse than the stand-in's 0.139.

choices.text: Both say it is badly calibrated
choices.why: Its number matches its rate exactly.

choices.text: ECE is zero; Brier still charges it
choices.why: Right: calibrated, and useless for telling which reply to trust.

choices.text: ECE needs more than one bin
choices.why: One bin is enough; its gap is zero.

prompt: `h04` stated 0.97 and was wrong. Why does one such reply move the Brier score so much more than a right reply stated at 0.97?

choices.text: Wrong replies are counted twice
choices.why: Every reply counts once.

choices.text: The gap is squared: 0.9409 against 0.0009
choices.why: Right: a confident mistake costs about a thousand times a confident success.

choices.text: Brier ignores right replies
choices.why: They add (0.97 − 1)², which is small but not zero.

choices.text: Brier uses bins, and `h04` sits in the largest bin, so its weight is multiplied by 34
choices.why: Brier uses no bins; that is ECE.

prompt: *On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks* (Guo and others, 2017) studied calibration. What did it find?
hint: Compare the networks of 2017 with older ones.

choices.text: Language models state well-calibrated confidences
choices.why: The paper was about classifiers' computed probabilities, not stated numbers.

choices.text: Larger networks were better calibrated
choices.why: The opposite: modern, deeper networks were more overconfident.

choices.text: Newer deep nets were more overconfident than older ones
choices.why: Right, and a single rescaling, temperature scaling, fixed much of it.

choices.text: Calibration cannot be measured without a person
choices.why: It needs labels, which people gave, and then it is arithmetic.

prompt: With the threshold at 0.80, what accuracy did the holdout set get on the replies it answered? Two decimal places.
hint: The `conf >= 0.80` line of the holdout run.

prompt: On dev, a threshold of 0.80 gave 39 answers at accuracy 1.00. On holdout it gave 22 at 0.68. What changed?
hint: Same model, same prompt, same threshold.

choices.text: The stand-in was sampled at a higher temperature on the holdout run, so its answers were noisier
choices.why: Both runs were at temperature 0.

choices.text: The messages: harder ones, many with evidence for two labels
choices.why: Right: exactly where the stand-in's rule overstates.

choices.text: The threshold was applied differently
choices.why: It is the same comparison, `conf >= 0.80`.

choices.text: The dev set was mislabelled
choices.why: Nothing suggests that; it is the easier set.

prompt: On the holdout, answering everything gives 0.57 and answering at 0.80 or above gives 0.68. What does that show about a miscalibrated confidence?
hint: A threshold uses the order of the numbers, not their values.

choices.text: It is useless and should be thrown away
choices.why: It still raised accuracy by holding eight messages back.

choices.text: It still ranks answers usefully
choices.why: Right: the ranking helps; the stated accuracy does not hold.

choices.text: It becomes calibrated above 0.80
choices.why: Above 0.80 it still says about 0.85 to 0.96 and delivers 0.68.

choices.text: The holdout is too small to say anything
choices.why: It is small, and the difference from dev is still large.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson give as rules for a stated confidence? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three rules, the same as for any output.

choices.text: Measure it against labels a person gave
choices.why: Yes: reliability table, ECE and Brier.

choices.text: Choose a threshold on one set and report it on another
choices.why: Yes: the set you chose on is a best case.

choices.text: Re-measure when the prompt, the model or the messages change
choices.why: Yes: calibration belongs to all three together.

choices.text: Trust it once the model is large enough
choices.why: Size is not a measurement.

prompt: Put the steps of putting a confidence threshold into production in order.
items: Collect a stated confidence with every answer
Choose a threshold on one labelled set
Check that threshold on a second set
Re-measure when the prompt, model or messages change

prompt: Match each measure to the question it answers.

pairs.right: Can I read the number as a rate?
Does the number separate good answers from bad?
Where, bin by bin, is the gap?
How many to answer, and how many of those right?

right_distractors: How many tokens does each call cost?

prompt: A vendor says its model's stated confidence is calibrated, citing an ECE of 0.02 on its own benchmark. What do you do before routing your messages by it?
hint: Whose messages was that measured on?

choices.text: Use 0.98 as the threshold, since the ECE is 0.02
choices.why: ECE is an average gap, not a threshold.

choices.text: Trust it: 0.02 is very small
choices.why: Small on their messages; the stand-in went from 0.092 to 0.282 between two sets.

choices.text: Ask for the Brier score instead
choices.why: Another number on their benchmark answers the same wrong question.

choices.text: Measure it on your own labelled messages
choices.why: Right: calibration belongs to the model, the prompt and the messages together.
